docs.title: Introduction to CTFs
docs.text:
Capture The Flags (CTFs) are cybersecurity challenges designed to help people learn and practice different security concepts in a practical way.

These challenges usually involve:

  • Linux basics
  • Networking
  • Cryptography
  • Web exploitation
  • Reverse engineering
  • Forensics
  • Scripting and automation

Most challenges require finding a hidden flag in the format:

flag{example_flag}

docs.title: How I Started
docs.text:
I started learning cybersecurity mainly through beginner-friendly CTF platforms like:

  • picoCTF
  • CyLab Security Academy

These platforms helped me understand:

  • how to approach challenges
  • basic Linux commands
  • enumeration techniques
  • problem solving methodology

At the beginning, even simple challenges felt confusing because I didn’t know:

  • which tools to use
  • where to start
  • how to analyze files
  • how to search for clues

Over time, I slowly became more comfortable with:

  • using Linux
  • reading challenge descriptions carefully
  • checking files and outputs
  • researching unfamiliar concepts

docs.title: Why I Started Writing Writeups
docs.text:
I created these writeups mainly to:

  • track my learning progress
  • revise solved challenges later
  • document tools and commands I used
  • improve my problem-solving approach

These writeups are written while learning, so some methods may not always be the most optimized ones.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
The goal is not only to solve challenges, but also to understand:

  • why a solution works
  • how vulnerabilities are identified
  • how different tools are used in real scenarios

“Every system has a weakness, the challenge is finding it first.” — Seplestr

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: If I told you a word started with 0x70 in hexadecimal, what would it start with in ASCII?

docs.title: Initial Thoughts
docs.text:
At first glance, the challenge immediately looked related to hexadecimal and ASCII conversion.

Since 0x70 is a hexadecimal value, I assumed the task was simply to convert it into its ASCII equivalent.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
I decided to check what character 0x70 represents in ASCII.

This can be done using:

  • an online ASCII table
  • Python
  • Linux terminal commands

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Using Python:

chr(0x70)

Output:

p

The hexadecimal value 0x70 corresponds to the character p in ASCII.

docs.title: What I Learned
docs.text:
• Basic hexadecimal to ASCII conversion
  • Understanding character encoding
  • Using Python for quick conversions
